reader_questions: Was maritime commerce two-way, and how do we know?
What can we reconstruct about boat construction and navigation?
Do population histories connect with Boita remembrance?

claims.evidence_boundary: What does your family place in its little boat, and what meaning does that act have for you? A household memory need not speak for every household.
Could this object have reached the port through an intermediary? What would distinguish a direct voyage from a chain of exchanges?
Which is being traced here: the rock, the anchor, or the vessel? Those journeys may be related without being identical.
What evidence would show people moving, rather than an object or an idea passing from hand to hand?
Was a boat intended to cross a lagoon, negotiate surf, work an estuary or sail offshore? Ask about its task before judging its shape.
Look at the seam between two boards: how is it joined, sealed and supported? That small detail can tell you more than the size of the boat.
When a model is labelled with a cargo capacity, what measurements and loading assumptions support that number?
What did a navigator need to know for the whole crossing, and what could only be learned about a particular harbour entrance?
Which question is a study answering: language history, ancestry, a migration route, a trading voyage or the history of a ritual? A strong connection must bridge those questions with evidence.

source_inspection.inspection_and_limits: Ministry of Culture, 6 February 2025. Release text rechecked 9 October 2026; used for contemporary commemoration, not proof of a particular ancient route or household participation rate.

Tripati and colleagues, Scientific Reports 12, 13559 (2022), DOI 10.1038/s41598-022-17910-9. Abstract, location and methods text inspected in the repository PDF on 9 October 2026. Nature’s page could not be fetched. No independent replication or exact voyage reconstruction claimed.

I. Wayan Ardika and Peter Bellwood, Antiquity 65 (1991), pages 221–232. ANU abstract and bibliographic record rechecked 9 October 2026; full paper not inspected in this review. Scope is India–Bali contact, not an exclusive Odisha origin.

Heritage 4, pp.806–815. Web-extracted abstract and excavation/ceramic discussion on pp.806 and 808 inspected; PDF screenshots failed. Used for reported finds, not unverified background claims about travellers or a universal port chronology.

Public-domain translation, cotton-fabrics passage inspected. Kalinga is named among valued producing regions. This does not identify a sea export, destination, date of a voyage or a modern Odisha commodity total; no single composition date is asserted.

Scientific Reports, DOI 10.1038/s41598-022-26799-3. Publisher text: abstract, archaeological context and methods inspected. One individual from Vat Komnou, directly dated 78–234 calCE; evidence of ancestry, not an Odisha attribution or a reconstruction of parental occupation.

Australasian Journal of Maritime Archaeology 42, pp.39–52, especially pp.41–42. Existing KB capture and its 4 October original-page inspection reused. Ratnagiri dating and equipment are the authors’ reading of religious imagery; no full hull or universal trader identification.

Author-uploaded chapter text re-read: nauka and padhua subsections. Later craft descriptions, not direct ancient Sadhaba specifications. Botanical identifications and broad naming equivalences are not adopted; upload date 2016 is not another study.

Language, Literature, Culture & Integrity, Vol.II, pp.22–32; editor-uploaded text, especially pp.23–28, inspected. Published observation and attributed fisherman testimony, not our fieldwork. Compare with Bhattacharya and Varadarajan’s 2001 study, DOI 10.4000/tc.304: its abstract was accessible, full text challenged; these overlapping accounts are not independent corroboration.

University Physics Vol.1, §14.4 inspected. Supports the modern displacement/loading explanation. Other engineering questions are explicitly general analysis, not a vessel-specific stability calculation or evidence that an ancient navigator used modern formulae.

Current Science 90(6), pp.864–871. Existing original-PDF capture reused; author-uploaded text re-read for seasonal interpretation. Festivals and environmental patterns are used in the paper’s reconstruction; no recovered sailing log. Mirror: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/27666817_Monsoon_wind_and_maritime_trade_A_case_study_of_historical_evidence_from_Orissa_India
Official explanation inspected. Larger new/full-moon tidal range is modern physical explanation, not historical proof of a Kartika departure rule.

Author-deposited ICAAL 8 presentation, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.3365316; full PDF text inspected, especially slides 4, 9–12, 16, 22–23. Related JSEALS 12(2), pp.35–57 paper: https://hdl.handle.net/10524/52454 (abstract indexed; journal full PDF not recovered). Slides and paper are one hypothesis lineage, not independent studies. Arrival route and language-contact model remain hypotheses.

Scientific Reports 9, 3818. Publisher abstract, methods and Results and Discussion inspected. Sampled Munda populations, model-dependent admixture dates; no maritime route inferred directly from a genome. Author correction, DOI 10.1038/s41598-019-42195-w, supplies the dataset accession GSE126882.

BMC Biology 19, 61. Updated publisher abstract and Discussion inspected. Alternative deep-history model, with acknowledged ancient-DNA gap. Split time is not admixture time. Publisher correction is linked at DOI 10.1186/s12915-021-01174-2; its separate text could not be retrieved, so no claim about its contents is made.

Author-posted version, labelled preprint/to appear, dated 2021 and uploaded 2022. Introduction and relevant distribution discussion inspected. Challenges the proposed maximal geographic spread; not presented as a conclusive disproof of maritime arrival. Final journal version not inspected.

exclusions: No common foreign origin asserted for all Odisha tribal communities.
No ancient migration assigned to Sadhaba voyages or Boita Bandana without bridging evidence.
No identification of prehistoric archaeological cultures with named modern communities.
No universal boat design, cargo manifest, barter-only economy, passenger identity or ancient capacity.
Behera 2016 background claims about Xuanzang sailing from Kalinga and Java migration inscriptions not adopted; ceramic findings used within scope.
Botanical inconsistencies in boat chapters omitted.
No new outreach, field confirmation, human review or search-index eligibility.
further_work: Recover full JSEALS paper and inspect linguistic reconstructions against primary language data; compare final Peterson version.
Seek site-level stratigraphy and securely dated cargo evidence before assigning direct routes.
Find catalogued boatbuilding manuscripts and hull remains; later craft comparison is not an excavated boita.
Commission no fieldwork: consented builder/practitioner work and specialist population-history review remain future tasks.
